nameStory: The smooth puffer gets its name from two key features that make it stand out from other pufferfish. Unlike many of its spiny relatives, this species has remarkably smooth skin without the rough bumps or spines you'd expect to feel on a pufferfish. The 'puffer' part comes from its incredible ability to inflate like a balloon when threatened, gulping water to transform from a normal fish into a spiky ball that's hard for predators to swallow.
description: The smooth puffer is a truly impressive fish that can grow up to 39 inches long, making it one of the largest pufferfish in the world. Despite its name suggesting otherwise, when inflated this fish is anything but smooth - it becomes a formidable spiky sphere. Most of the time though, you'll see it in its normal torpedo-shaped form, swimming alone or in small loose groups. This is a fish that spends most of its adult life in open ocean waters rather than close to shore, making encounters relatively rare in New England waters.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Large, torpedo-shaped body that can inflate into a spiky ball when threatened - if you see a fish suddenly puff up like a balloon, you've found a puffer

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Exceptionally large for a pufferfish, reaching over 3 feet in length - much bigger than the small puffers you might expect

idTips.label: Skin Texture
idTips.description: Skin feels surprisingly smooth to the touch when deflated, lacking the rough bumps or permanent spines of many other pufferfish

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found in open ocean waters rather than shallow bays or harbors, usually over sandy or muddy bottoms at moderate depths

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Small mouth with fused teeth that form a beak-like structure, perfect for crushing the shells of crustaceans and small fish

habitat: In New England waters, smooth puffers are found in offshore oceanic waters along the continental margin, typically over sandy or muddy bottoms. Adults prefer the open ocean environment at depths between 33 and 590 feet, while juveniles may venture closer to shore or near offshore banks. You're most likely to encounter them during deep-sea fishing trips rather than from shore or in shallow coastal waters.

seasonality.spring: Smooth puffers may move into New England waters as ocean temperatures warm, though sightings remain extremely rare with only 2 recorded observations in the region.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for potential encounters as warmer water temperatures make New England waters more suitable, though they remain in deeper offshore areas.
seasonality.fall: May still be present in offshore waters before retreating south as temperatures begin to drop, following their preferred temperature ranges.
seasonality.winter: Unlikely to be found in New England waters as they move to warmer southern waters, following their range that extends south to Argentina.

funFact: This massive pufferfish can be lethally toxic to eat - it contains the same deadly neurotoxin (tetrodotoxin) found in the famous Japanese fugu, which is 1,200 times more poisonous than cyanide and has no known antidote!
confusionNotes: The smooth puffer is sometimes confused with Lagocephalus inermis, but that species is found in the Indo-Pacific, not the Atlantic. In New England waters, its large size and smooth skin when deflated help distinguish it from smaller, bumpier pufferfish species that might occasionally visit our waters.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'pufferfish,' this species spends most of its time looking like a normal fish - the dramatic puffing behavior is a defense mechanism reserved for when they feel truly threatened. The inflation is achieved by rapidly gulping water (or air if caught), and they can take several minutes to deflate back to normal size.
compareHints: As the only Lagocephalus species documented in New England waters, the smooth puffer stands out from other regional pufferfish by its exceptional size and pelagic lifestyle. While other puffers in New England tend to be smaller coastal species, the smooth puffer is a true giant of the open ocean. Its smooth skin texture when deflated also contrasts with the permanently rough or spiny skin of most other pufferfish families.
